title: The State of Model Routing — NVIDIA, Cognition, OpenRouter
talk_summary: A panel of NVIDIA, Cognition (Devin), and OpenRouter engineers discuss model routing: keeping a frontier model as orchestrator while delegating implementation to cheaper models, the fragility of naive task-type routing, and the token/cache economics of multi-model systems. Key mechanisms include a persistent 'sidekick' sub-agent with warm cache, context compaction for handoffs, and using cache-refresh cadence as a free opportunity to have the big model sanity-check the small one.

takeaways.technique: Frontier orchestrator + cheap executor (not naive task-type routing)
takeaways.what_they_do: Keep a frontier model doing planning and hard decisions, delegate implementation to cheaper models; the frontier model stays watching so it can pull work back when the small model is out of its depth.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we allow Fable to still do like the planning and the the hard decision making but delegate a lot of the work to an implementation model

takeaways.technique: Avoid naive per-task-type routing; route by phase/complexity
takeaways.what_they_do: They warn that routing purely by task type is fragile because agentic tasks change complexity mid-run (explore -> implement -> debug); the router must track phases and let the smart model detect when a sub-model is out of depth.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this kind of like naive like initial routing to based on the task type is extremely fragile, especially the more agentic the task

takeaways.technique: Small models can be more expensive out-of-domain (token thrash)
takeaways.what_they_do: They cite that a small model can burn far more tokens looping on out-of-distribution tasks, making it costlier than a big model despite lower per-token price.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Opus will do about three times better at 1/10 the cost of Haiku, even though Haiku's significantly cheaper per token
takeaways.numbers: Opus ~3x better at 1/10 the cost of Haiku on terminal-bench

takeaways.technique: Persistent 'sidekick' sub-agent with warm cache instead of fresh sub-agents
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of spawning fresh sub-agents (which re-read files and re-pay context), they keep one sidekick with a continuously running context so the main agent doesn't re-provide context and cache stays warm; roles can swap.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we don't use sub agents. We use what we call a sidekick, which is um, one sub agent that continually has a running context

takeaways.technique: Compaction for handoffs + reference-by-file instead of dumping context
takeaways.what_they_do: When handing off between models, pass compacted context or file references rather than full traces; big models are token-efficient at reading only what they need. Note compaction causes a cache miss, so compact mainly for intelligence, not cost.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of dumping the full thing, it just references them by file

takeaways.technique: Use cache-refresh cadence as a free frontier sanity-check
takeaways.what_they_do: Since KV caches expire on a ~5-minute cadence anyway, they piggyback a frontier-model check ('is the small model going down a rabbit hole?') on the refresh, getting a big-model call nearly free.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you basically can get a free like big like frontier model call uh if you kind of like ask the right question
